source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: A process analysis. Int J Man-Machine Studies 23:459-494
finding: Founding study. Verbal-protocol study of how programmers debug one COBOL program. Expertise was NOT given in advance. It was derived after the fact from how well each person 'chunked' the program, measured by how smoothly their debugging flowed.
numbers: 16 programmers from one organisation (8 'experts', 8 'novices'). Task: one COBOL sales-report program with control breaks, one logic bug, two versions (high bug and low bug, 4+4 experts and novices on each). Talk-aloud protocols coded by hand.
quote: the criterion of expertise was the subjects' ability to chunk effectively the program they were required to debug
limits: Exploratory. N=16, one program, one language, one organisation. Author states the propositions are 'for further testing'.
agent_relevance: Source of the hypothesis. Expertise here is a process pattern (few switches, few revisits), not a score. Our agent can measure the same pattern in its own trace in code.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: A process analysis. Int J Man-Machine Studies 23:459-494
finding: Chunking was operationalised with three counts: (1) number of changes between debugging functions, (2) number of reversions to the top 'Debug program' function, (3) number of changes of location in the program (data division, procedure modules, input and output listings). More of each means weaker chunking.
numbers: Each subject ranked on the three variables. 11 of 16 subjects got the same class on all three; 3 got it on a 2:1 basis; 2 were ties. One borderline subject (EL2) was made an expert only to keep 8 vs 8 groups. Position-change counts were adjusted for bug level.
limits: Classification used a ranking procedure that forced 8 vs 8. The classifying variables are also process variables, so later 'experts show smoother processes' findings are partly circular.
agent_relevance: A usable code-checked trace metric: count mode switches, re-reads of the same part, and location jumps. Compare against a budget instead of asking the model if it is 'confident'.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: A process analysis. Int J Man-Machine Studies 23:459-494
finding: The process-based (chunking) classification beat the manager's rating at predicting performance. Managers rated mostly by years of experience, not ability.
numbers: Ex post chunking classification explained 73.7% of variance in debug time; manager classification explained 36.1%. Mean debug time: experts 15 min 40 s vs novices 28 min 3 s (chunking class); 20 min 24 s vs 23 min 19 s (manager class). The two classifications agreed on only 10 of 16 subjects. All 5 people who made incorrect changes were novices by chunking class; managers put only 4 of the 5 in the novice group.
limits: Classification was derived from the same data it is then tested on. Author admits test-retest reliability of the method was never checked.
agent_relevance: Supports 'process quality beats seniority labels'. Do not assign roles to agent samples by claimed experience; judge by trace behaviour.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: A process analysis. Int J Man-Machine Studies 23:459-494
finding: Outcome and process differences between chunking-classified experts and novices. Novices needed more time, more phases, more episodes, more looks at the faulty module, more modules, and made more errors. Time per episode did NOT differ.
numbers: Total time: novices slower, P<0.001 (R2=0.737); bug effect P=0.001 (low bug slower); interaction. Time to discover error P=0.005 (R2=0.572). Major phases P=0.001 (R2=0.712). Episodes P=0.003 (R2=0.570). Modules examined P=0.045 (R2=0.299). Times module B000 examined P=0.007. Mistakes: novices more, P=0.005 (R2=0.500). Average time per episode: no significant effect. Number of hypotheses: novices more, P=0.045 (R2=0.230).
limits: ANOVA/ANCOVA with 2 factors on 16 people; several tests with no correction; p-values near 0.045 are fragile.
agent_relevance: Experts did not think faster per step; they took fewer steps. For an agent, the saving comes from fewer episodes and revisits, not faster tokens.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: A process analysis. Int J Man-Machine Studies 23:459-494
finding: Breadth-first vs depth-first was defined by whether a person was 'constrained' by an early hypothesis. Constrained, hypothesis-led searchers were depth-first and were all novices. Those who let the program structure unfold, kept constraints open, and built a model were breadth-first.
numbers: 9 of 16 stated hypotheses (1 to 3 each); 19 hypotheses in total (3 control-break, 5 resetting previous numbers, 9 clearing DETAIL-LINE, 2 resetting the change flag). Constrained subjects: NH1, NL2, NL3, NL4, all novices. Two novices (NL2, NL3) used a 'shotgun' approach of continual random edits.
quote: They do not permit the formulation of hypotheses to lead them to a depth-first search for the error.
limits: Depth-first here is a coder judgement about commitment to a hypothesis, not a measured search order. Only 4 clearly constrained subjects.
agent_relevance: Matches guardrail G1 and G2: do not lock onto the first hypothesis; keep alternatives open until real output refutes them. 'Shotgun edits' is the failure mode to detect and block in code.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: A process analysis. Int J Man-Machine Studies 23:459-494
finding: Two binary conditions (breadth-first search for the error; system thinking) reproduced the chunking-based expert/novice split for 15 of 16 people. Breadth-first without a system model still produced mistakes and counted as novice.
numbers: Decision table with 2 binary conditions classified 15 of 16 subjects the same as chunking class. Only subject NH2 differed. Strategy paths: 6 of 16 possible paths used. Subjects NL1, NH3, NH4 judged deficient in system thinking; NL1 took about twice as long to build the model (25 min 12 s total, error named at 13 min 32 s).
limits: Same 16 subjects; convergence between two author-defined measures is not independent validation.
agent_relevance: Expert pattern = open search AND an explicit model of how the program works before declaring a fix. Fits a schema step: build a model state first, then locate the fault, then confirm.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: A process analysis. Int J Man-Machine Studies 23:459-494
finding: The abstract's proposition 2(a) says novices ALSO use breadth-first but lack system thinking, while 2(b) says novices use depth-first. These are two novice types, not one claim. The abstract wording 'experts breadth-first, novices depth-first' is a simplification.
numbers: Propositions 1(a),1(b),2(a),2(b),2(c) all listed 'for further testing'. No statistical test of the propositions themselves was done.
quote: Novices use breadth-first approaches to debugging but are deficient in their ability to think in system terms
limits: Propositions were generated from the same data, never tested in the paper.
agent_relevance: Do not cite this as established. Repo note says 'hypothesis, not established'; this confirms it from the primary text.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: A process analysis. Int J Man-Machine Studies 23:459-494
finding: Things that did NOT separate experts from novices: looking at program output first, reading modules versus mentally executing them, number of DATA DIVISION items examined, and time per episode. The study found no support for a formal symptom-pattern-recognition feature as seen in medical diagnosis.
numbers: Data-division items examined: no difference (R2=0.104). Output-first vs program-first: no effect on problem solving. Bug level mattered for time and for module re-examination (P=0.023) but not for strategy.
limits: Null results on N=16 have low power.
agent_relevance: Where the agent starts reading (output or code) is not the key lever. Do not build a rule for it.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: A process analysis. Int J Man-Machine Studies 23:459-494
finding: Vessey's own list of limits: the classification method has never been tested for reliability; one program, one task, a simple business domain chosen so domain knowledge would not matter. She cites Brooks (1977) that a typical programmer may hold about 50,000 chunks.
numbers: 50,000 chunks estimate is Brooks 1977 as cited; not measured here.
limits: Single task and language (COBOL, 1980s batch reporting). Experts in other domains may chunk differently.
agent_relevance: Do not transfer the 'expert is smooth' pattern to hard novel bugs without a test.

source: Detienne (1990) as above, reporting Shneiderman (1976)
finding: Classic recall result as reported in a review: experts recall programs better than novices when lines are in correct order, and this advantage disappears when the lines are scrambled. This is the programming version of the chess recall pattern.
numbers: No numbers given in the secondary source I read. Original not opened.
limits: Second-hand. Needs the original Shneiderman 1976 paper (Int J Computer and Information Sciences) for N and recall percentages.
agent_relevance: A test the agent can run on itself: does a model recall or use a program better in coherent form than shuffled? A gap means it uses learned structure, not line-by-line reading.

source: Detienne (1990) Expert programming knowledge: a schema-based approach (in Hoc, Green, Samurcay, Gilmore, Psychology of Programming), reporting Adelson (1981)
finding: Recall-based categorisation: novices grouped program parts by surface and syntactic features; experts grouped parts by function and by procedural similarity. Experts therefore chunk by what code does, but also keep control-structure groupings, which fits a control-flow account too.
numbers: No numbers in the secondary source. Original not opened.
limits: Second-hand summary. Only one reported interpretation.
agent_relevance: Define a 'chunk' for the agent by function (what the part does), not by syntax or line count.

source: Detienne (1990) Expert programming knowledge: a schema-based approach (in Hoc, Green, Samurcay, Gilmore, Psychology of Programming), reporting Soloway and Ehrlich (1984)
finding: Plan-like vs unplan-like programs, fill-in-the-blank task with one deleted line and no statement of purpose. Experts beat novices; plan-like beat unplan-like; and there was an interaction: breaking the programming conventions hurt experts more than novices. Experts also tended to give the plan-like answer even for unplan-like code.
numbers: Direction of effects only; no cell means in the review. Original not opened.
limits: Second-hand. Tests schema/plan knowledge, which is a close cousin of chunking but not the same.
agent_relevance: Expert-style pattern matching gives errors when code breaks convention. Strong risk for an LLM too: plausible-answer completion can override what the code says (supports G2, G3).

source: Detienne (1990) Expert programming knowledge: a schema-based approach (in Hoc, Green, Samurcay, Gilmore, Psychology of Programming), reporting Detienne (1984, 1986) debugging and recall experiments
finding: Experts evoked programming plans from cues (variable names, initialisations) and drew inferences. In recall they distorted code toward schema defaults: recalled counter I instead of J, 'while' for 'repeat', and inserted a 'creation' function that was not in the program. Experts missed errors when they strongly expected a value and did not check it.
numbers: Protocol rules: 269 production rules coded, grouped into 47 general rules. N not given in the review.
limits: Review chapter; small expert samples; Pascal programs.
agent_relevance: The cost of chunking: an expectation filled in without a check. Same as model 'hallucinated fill'. Revise only from real output (G2); require a check that the expected value exists in the text.

source: Detienne (1990) Expert programming knowledge: a schema-based approach (in Hoc, Green, Samurcay, Gilmore, Psychology of Programming), reporting Pennington (1987)
finding: Boundary condition against pure plan/chunk-by-function. In one study, control-flow questions were answered faster and more correctly than data-flow or function questions, and recognition was faster within the same control structure than within the same functional structure. Language mattered: COBOL programmers did better on data flow, Fortran programmers on control flow. After a modification task comprehension shifted toward function and data flow.
numbers: No cell numbers in the review.
limits: Second-hand; comprehension task changes the mental model, so chunk type is task dependent.
agent_relevance: Chunk type depends on the goal. Let the program pick the view (control or data flow) from the task state rather than fixing one.

source: Detienne (1990) Expert programming knowledge: a schema-based approach (in Hoc, Green, Samurcay, Gilmore, Psychology of Programming), reporting Rist (1986) and Norcio (1982)
finding: Rist: asked to group lines that 'did the same thing', novices used a mix of syntactic and plan chunks; experts used almost only plan chunks; plan use fell for complex programs. Norcio: indenting by functional chunks raised correct fill-in; a comment before a chunk helped when the blank was at the start of a chunk.
numbers: Norcio: indented group supplied significantly more correct statements (no figures in review). Rist: no figures.
limits: Second-hand; small studies of the 1980s.
agent_relevance: Format the agent's working notes so chunk boundaries are explicit and chunk-start cues are present. Cheap prompt-side aid.

source: Detienne (1990) Expert programming knowledge: a schema-based approach (in Hoc, Green, Samurcay, Gilmore, Psychology of Programming) (section on tasks)
finding: Theory contrast. Schema-based (Soloway, Brooks, Rich): understanding is evoking and instantiating plans from memory, bottom-up or top-down. Control-flow (Shneiderman and Mayer syntactic/semantic model, Pennington, Atwood and Ramsey): identify control structures, merge into larger ones until functions emerge. Detienne concludes understanding may be schema-based or control-based depending on situation and plan fit.
numbers: n/a (theory review).
limits: 1990 review; neither side tested with strong controls.
agent_relevance: Two chunking routes: recognise a known plan (fast, fallible) or compose from control flow (slow, safer). A router in code can choose by familiarity signal, with simulation as fallback when no cue fires.

source: Wyrich (2023) Source code comprehension: a contemporary definition and conceptual model (history section)
finding: History of the bottom-up chunking model. Shneiderman and Mayer (1979): programmers recognise the function of groups of statements and join these chunks into larger ones until the whole program is understood. Brooks (1983) added top-down hypotheses and coined 'beacons'. Adelson: experts have larger recall chunks with more semantic content. Wiedenbeck: beacons help mainly experienced developers.
numbers: No numbers in the history section.
quote: programmers recognize the function of groups of statements, and then piece together these chunks to form even larger chunks
limits: Secondary history; claims about each study are as the author summarises them.
agent_relevance: Gives the lineage Vessey sits in: chunking is the cognitive core, beacons are the cue that triggers a chunk.

source: Wyrich (2023) Source code comprehension: a contemporary definition and conceptual model (history section), reporting Crosby et al. (2002) eye tracking and Letovsky/Littman (1986)
finding: At least two beacon types: single mnemonic lines and complex beacons that signal main goals. Experts rely on beacons, novices do not. Littman et al.: programmers who did systematic symbolic execution of data-flow paths built 'strong' mental models and succeeded more at modification than as-needed readers.
numbers: O'Brien et al.: eight industrial developers; expectation-based and inference-based comprehension both used alongside bottom-up. Letovsky: six professional developers thinking aloud.
limits: Small N throughout; second-hand.
agent_relevance: Strong model (static plus causal knowledge) needs execution traces, not only reading. Supports running code to learn, rather than judging by text alone.

source: Siegmund et al. (2017) Measuring neural efficiency of program comprehension. ESEC/FSE
finding: fMRI test linking semantic chunking and beacons. Bottom-up comprehension (no usable cues) activated BA 39 and BA 6, 21, 40, 44; comprehension with semantic cues activated these areas significantly less, and BA 39 was deactivated. The authors read this as evidence for semantic chunking in bottom-up reading and for neural efficiency when beacons exist.
numbers: 11 participants; 12 trials each; bottom-up condition (obfuscated names, scrambled layout) vs 4 semantic-cue conditions plus a syntax-error control; each task about 30 s; random-effects GLM, p<0.01 FDR corrected. Response times did not differ across conditions by design.
quote: We found evidence of semantic chunking during bottom-up comprehension and lower activation of brain areas during comprehension based on semantic cues
limits: Tiny N; participants were primed with the snippets before scanning; expected memory-area activation for plans was NOT found; the authors speculate low expertise or plans sharing comprehension circuits; resting condition overlaps the default network.
agent_relevance: Weak neuro support only. The cue-versus-no-cue contrast says what to test in the agent: same code with meaningful vs stripped names, measure accuracy and tokens.

source: Siegmund et al. (2017) replication of the earlier fMRI bottom-up study (same paper, RQ1)
finding: Partial replication of the earlier bottom-up fMRI study: the main brain areas were found again, and the authors say they 'largely replicate' it. Extra areas (BA 21, BA 44) activated and BA 6 appeared at a slightly different location.
numbers: Same significance threshold as the original (p<0.01 FDR). Original N not read here.
limits: Differences in location of BA 6; the replication shared authors with the original.
agent_relevance: Brain evidence for chunking is consistent but thin; do not use it as a design argument.

source: Le, Nguyen, Nguyen (2026) Do machines struggle where humans do? LLM and human comprehension of obfuscated code
finding: LLMs on obfuscated code. Obfuscation strips the beacons and structure that humans use to chunk. Reasoning-tuned small models track which tasks humans find hard; coder-tuned and instruct models do not. No model reproduces the human expert pattern of doing better under moderate (misleading-name) obfuscation.
numbers: 12 models (0.5B to 8B) incl. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, SmolLM3-3B, Phi-4-mini, Qwen3-0.6B, CodeLlama-7B, DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B, Llama-3.1-8B. Spearman with human task accuracy: Phi-4-mini 0.47, SmolLM3-3B 0.36, DS-R1-Qwen-7B 0.37, Qwen3-0.6B 0.30 (all p<=0.003); Llama-3.1-8B 0.08, CodeLlama-7B 0.02, DS-Coder-6.7B 0.10 (n.s.). Human base: 50 undergraduates, 20 function-level output-prediction tasks, 5 tiers.
limits: Preprint (arXiv 2606.31725, 30 Jun 2026), only models up to 8B, small human baseline of undergraduates; accuracy is exact output match.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM evidence on cue removal. Near-floor coder-tuned models mean these tasks measure reasoning more than pattern recall.

source: Le, Nguyen, Nguyen (2026) Do machines struggle where humans do? LLM and human comprehension of obfuscated code
finding: Accuracy under obfuscation tiers, models vs humans. Best model DS-R1-Qwen-7B fell from 63.8% to 51.8% when adversarial (misleading) names were used (L1b) and to 56.2% at the full combination (L3). Human experts did the opposite and peaked at L1b, read as reliance on structure over names.
numbers: DS-R1-Qwen-7B: L0 63.8, L1 64.2, L1b 51.8, L2 57.0, L3 56.2 (%). SmolLM3-3B: 45, 44, 34, 38, 33. CodeLlama-7B 12.4, 13.2, 9.6, 10.8, 11.4. Llama-3.1-8B 16, 23, 12, 17, 20. Instruct models showed a sensitivity peak at L1b under System-2 prompting.
limits: Tiers are not strictly monotonic; GLMM with random snippet and model effects; one human study as baseline.
agent_relevance: LLMs lean on name cues (beacons) more than human experts do. Misleading names are a test of whether the agent rechecks against real behaviour (G2, G3).

source: Le, Nguyen, Nguyen (2026) Do machines struggle where humans do? LLM and human comprehension of obfuscated code
finding: Reasoning-trace length as an effort proxy: longer chain-of-thought goes with lower accuracy; wrong answers are not significantly longer once snippet and model are controlled. Prompting for System-2 plus one example lifted all models; a working-memory-tax prompt had negligible effect.
numbers: Spearman rho=-0.520 (p=1.11e-4); Pearson r=-0.515 (p=1.32e-4) between mean accuracy and mean CoT tokens. Incorrect answers above 1,000 tokens in L1-L3 but p=0.33 after controls. Mean tokens L1 1,011.4 vs L1b 1,014.4. Strong models collapse under low token limits (OR=12.5, 95% CI 6.4-24.2, p<0.001).
limits: Small models only; the working-memory tax test may not match human chunking limits.
agent_relevance: Long traces signal difficulty or confusion, not progress. A step budget triggered by trace growth is a defensible code-level check.

source: Kou, Chen, Wang, Ma, Zhang (2024) Do large language models pay similar attention like human programmers when generating code? Proc ACM Softw Eng 1(FSE):100
finding: Models do not attend to the same parts of a task description as human programmers. Human programmers labelled the important words; across six LLMs and twelve attention methods there was consistent misalignment. 27% of 211 wrong programs were explained by five attention patterns. Perturbation-based attention was closest to human labels and preferred by humans.
numbers: Six LLMs: GPT-4, InCoder-1.3B, CodeGen-2.7B, PolyCoder-2.7B, CodeParrot-1.5B, GPT-J-6B. User study 22 programmers (mean 5.62 years experience). Labelled keyword types: property 45.2%, operators 27.2%, conditional 25%, data types 2.6%.
limits: Measures reading of the problem statement, not code chunking. Attention weights are a weak proxy for reasoning.
agent_relevance: Indirect. What a model treats as the key chunk of a spec differs from what an expert picks; a restate-and-extract step checked by code (not self-grading) could reduce this.

source: Wang et al. (2023, v5 2024) How does naming affect LLMs on code analysis tasks?
finding: CodeBERT code search and clone detection collapse when identifiers are anonymised. Method definition names matter most. Java code search degrades most when all name types are changed. So code models lean on names as beacons.
numbers: Code search MRR: Java original 70.36%, as low as about 17.03% with all names anonymised; Python original 68.17%, about 23.7-24.1% with all names anonymised. Clone detection F1: Java original 94.87%, about 84.8-86.8% with all names changed.
limits: Table text in the PDF is partly garbled so exact cell values are approximate; CodeBERT is an encoder, not a chat LLM; only a small GPT case study.
agent_relevance: Names carry the chunk. If the agent must reason about code with bad names, add a rename-by-function step and check by running.

source: Glasz et al. (2025) Can LLMs replace humans during code chunking? MITRE
finding: Engineering sense of chunking, not Vessey's. LLM-created code partitions matched human expert split points best of all chunking methods on legacy MUMPS and assembly (ALC) files, and gave documentation comments up to 20% more factual and 10% more useful than human partitions in some model and corpus cells.
numbers: Four LLMs: GPT-4o, Claude 3 Sonnet, Mixtral, Llama 3. Ground truth: expert human partition points. Intra-class correlation of the GPT-4o judge across 10 runs: 0.960 (MUMPS) and 0.908 (ALC). Context length correlated positively with comment accuracy on MUMPS (rho=0.199, p=8.8e-10) but not on ALC, where full-file input scored lowest. Mixtral and Llama 3 scored 20-40 points lower on hallucination than GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 3.
limits: Quality scored by an LLM judge (GPT-4o), which the schema says to distrust; legacy languages only; human ground truth sparse for ALC; abstract figures are 'up to'.
agent_relevance: Splitting code at meaningful boundaries beats arbitrary splitting for LLMs. Chunk-by-structure is a real lever when inputs exceed context.

source: Cross-source check across Vessey (1985) and the later reviews and LLM papers read
finding: Gap found. In the sources I could open, I found no published test of Vessey's propositions on LLM agents, and no LLM study that uses scrambled-versus-ordered code recall or Vessey chunk-switch counts. The nearest work is obfuscation (Le 2026), naming (Wang 2023) and chunk-splitting for context (Glasz 2025). My search budget ran out, so this is not proof of absence.
numbers: Searches used: 2 of 6 allowed WebSearch (a third was refused, budget exhausted); arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs were rate-limited or empty.
limits: Absence claim is weak. Needs a follow-up search of 2023-2026 work on LLM code recall, shuffled-code reading, and trace analysis.
agent_relevance: The hypothesis is untested for LLMs. Treat as [S]/[D] and test it with our own trace metrics before adding any operator.

source: Cross-source synthesis of Vessey (1985) with Detienne (1990)
finding: Competing explanations for expert smoothness. (a) Vessey: better chunking means fewer returns. (b) Hypothesis commitment: novices lock on one idea; experts do not. (c) Vessey speculates experts have automated their problem solving, so they state fewer hypotheses. (d) Detienne: schema evocation gives speed but creates unchecked expectations.
numbers: None; interpretation only.
limits: No study separates these explanations; Vessey's data cannot, since the groups are defined by the process variables.
agent_relevance: A scaffold should copy the observable behaviours (low revisits, open hypotheses, model before fix, check expected values) and not rely on any one theory being right.
